te: A message comes on your phone. Your credit card payment is overdue.
Then another message. Then a call from a number you don't know.
In our last video, we saw how paying only the minimum keeps you in debt for years. Today, a harder question.
What if you cannot pay even that minimum?
Maybe your salary stopped. Maybe a hospital bill came first. It happens to good, honest people.
And then the fear starts. Will the police come home? Will they take my salary? Will my family find out?
Most people think there is one answer for everyone. There isn't.
Someone who owes ten thousand rupees and someone who owes ten lakh live two very different stories.
Today I will show you both. The rules on paper, and the reality on the ground.
Welcome to Be Practical with Kishore.
First, let's understand the clock. The day your last date passes, the bank starts counting.
Thirty days. Sixty days. Ninety days. The bank's system checks your account every single day.
If the minimum stays unpaid for ninety days after the due date, the bank must mark your card a bad loan. They call it an NPA. A non performing asset.
Now here is something most people don't know. From that day, your unpaid card is also a loss for the bank.
The bank must keep aside at least a quarter of what you owe, from its own profit. That is one reason the pressure grows around this time.
But listen carefully. Some people say interest stops after ninety days. No rule says that.
The bank cannot count your unpaid interest as its income. But your bill can keep growing as per your card terms.
There is a second clock too. Your CIBIL. Banks now update the credit bureaus every fifteen days.
The good part is, the bank must tell you before it reports you as a defaulter. And if you have a genuine dispute, it must wait.
In one case, a consumer commission held SBI Card at fault for reporting a customer to CIBIL without proper notice first.
And the card itself? At SBI Card, for example, it may be blocked from the very first missed payment.
Now the part nobody tells you. A small bill grows faster than a big bill.
Take two people. Ravi owes ten thousand rupees. Sunita owes one lakh. Both stop paying.
Both pay the same interest. Three point seven five percent a month, plus eighteen percent GST on it.
But the late fee is not a percentage. It is a fixed amount by slab. On ten thousand, the late fee is seven hundred and fifty rupees. On one lakh, it is thirteen hundred.
Seven hundred and fifty on ten thousand is seven and a half percent, every month, just as a fee. Thirteen hundred on one lakh is only one point three percent.
After six months of paying nothing, Ravi's ten thousand becomes about nineteen thousand. Almost double.
Sunita's one lakh becomes about one lakh thirty eight thousand.
For Ravi, about two thirds of that jump is late fees and the GST on them. So the smaller your bill, the harder the fees hit.
This is our own calculation, using one bank's published fees. Your bill will be different, but the shape is the same.
Now the real question. Who actually comes after you? And will anyone come to your house?
In the first three months, it is mostly calls. Automated calls, SMS, WhatsApp. Many from big call centres in cities.
Banks decide how hard to chase by two things. The days you are late, and the money at risk.
After that, many banks hand your account to a recovery agency. And here is the business behind it.
Many agencies earn only when they collect. A percentage of what you pay. One public sector bank pays its agencies between seven and a half and fifteen percent on accounts up to one lakh.
